propositions.text: Claimants are Afghan citizens seeking protection under IRPA Sections 96 and 97.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX XXXX and the person whom she alleges is her son, XXXX XXXX XXXX, the minor claimant, are citizens of Afghanistan. They claim protection under Sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

propositions.text: Claimant alleges relationship to minor as her son.
propositions.quote: the person whom she alleges is her son, XXXX XXXX XXXX, the minor claimant

paragraphs.summary: The claimants are Afghan citizens seeking protection under IRPA Sections 96 and 97; claimant alleges the minor is her son.

propositions.text: Claimant is from Kabul, was a XXXX, husband worked XXXX projects.
propositions.quote: The claimant is from Kabul. She was a XXXX, and her husband worked XXXX XXXX XXXX projects.

propositions.text: Husband received threatening calls from Taliban Commander XXXX to leave jobs with puppet government in 2011.
propositions.quote: On XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX, 2011 her husband received threatening phone calls from the local well-known Taliban Commander XXXX to leave their jobs with the puppet government.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant from Kabul, was a XXXX; husband worked on projects and received Taliban threats in 2011, claimant alleges.

propositions.text: In 2011 husband spoke to smuggler about Canada; in 2012 he went to brothers for money but never returned.
propositions.quote: On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2011 they moved and her husband spoke to a smuggler about coming to Canada. In XXXX 2012, he went to visit his brothers to get more money from land sales, but he never came back.

propositions.text: Claimant believes husband was taken by Taliban Commander XXXX; police told her to report to another province but she did not.
propositions.quote: She believes he was taken by Commander XXXX. She went to the police in Kabul but they said to report to XXXX province, but she did not because they were scheduled to leave.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant alleges husband disappeared after 2012 visit; believes Taliban took him; police advised reporting elsewhere but she did not.

propositions.text: Claimants are not Convention refugees under Section 96; no well-founded fear of persecution on Convention grounds.
propositions.quote: The Panel finds the claimants not to be Convention refugees under Section 96,2 as they do not have a well-founded fear of persecution in Afghanistan on any of the five Convention grounds.

propositions.text: Claimants are not persons in need of protection under Section 97; removal would not subject them to risk to life or cruel treatment.
propositions.quote: The Panel also finds that the claimants are not persons in need of protection under section 97,3 as, on a balance of probabilities, their removal to Afghanistan would not subject them personally to a risk to life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or to a danger of torture.

propositions.text: Panel will provide reasons for its findings.
propositions.quote: The Panel's reasons are as follows.

paragraphs.summary: Panel finds claimants not refugees or in need of protection under IRPA Sections 96 and 97; reasons follow.

propositions.text: Claimant gave most oral testimony; minor claimant questioned at hearing end.
propositions.quote: The claimant gave the great majority of the oral testimony. Counsel questioned the minor claimant at the end of the hearing.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant gave most testimony; minor questioned at hearing end.

propositions.text: Panel considered identity, credibility, well-foundedness of fear, risk to life, and all evidence and submissions.
propositions.quote: The Panel considered the issues of identity, credibility and the well-foundedness of the claimants' alleged fear of persecution, risk to life, etc., i.e., objective basis. The Panel considered all the evidence as well as counsel's oral submission at the close of the hearing.

paragraphs.summary: Panel considered identity, credibility, well-foundedness, and all evidence and submissions.

propositions.text: Claimants are Afghan citizens per passports, but claimant failed to prove husband is minor's father or that they are married.
propositions.quote: The Panel accepts that the claimants are citizens of Afghanistan, from the copies of their Afghani passports supplied. However, the claimant could not establish that her alleged husband (her "husband") is in fact the father of the minor.

propositions.text: Husband's name not on claimant's ID; on minor's ID only; no marriage or birth certificates provided.
propositions.quote: Their mutual husband / father's name was not listed on their passports. On the taskera (National ID document) of the claimant, her husband's name is not mentioned. It is mentioned on the minor's taskera, though. The claimant could supply no marriage certificate nor birth certificate for the minor.

propositions.text: Names of claimant and minor dissimilar; claimant's stated age at birth inconsistent with birthdates.
propositions.quote: The names of the claimant and the minor are in no part similar to each other. The claimant was asked how old she was when she gave birth to her son, and she said she was 37-38. However, as per the respective birthdates, the claimant would have been almost exactly 40, plus three days, when she gave birth to the minor.

propositions.text: Panel finds claimants are not mother and son; no post-hearing document requests made.
propositions.quote: All the factors lead the Panel to find that the claimants are not mother and son. The Panel notes at this time that neither counsel nor claimant requested time, post-hearing, to provide further documents, missing as of the hearing, which might have assisted their claim.

paragraphs.summary: Panel finds claimants are Afghan citizens but not mother and son; no marriage or birth certificates; no post-hearing documents requested.

propositions.text: Claimant could not document route to Canada or presence in Afghanistan after 2011; arrival date unknown.
propositions.quote: The claimant could not document any part of their alleged route to Canada, nor that they were even in Afghanistan at any time after XXXX 2011. The alleged key events occurred later in 2011. The claimants did not make their refugee claims at the airport in Canada, so it is impossible to document when they arrived.

propositions.text: Possible claimants were outside Afghanistan after 2011; Panel lacked full analysis ability on prior claims or delays.
propositions.quote: Thus, it is possible the claimants were somewhere else than Afghanistan later in 2011. Thus, the Panel may have been deprived of the ability to conduct a full analysis of issues such as failure to, and previous claim, elsewhere, and delay in claiming in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant failed to document route or presence in Afghanistan after 2011; possible absence deprives Panel of full analysis.

propositions.text: Claimant alleges she was a XXXX, supported by Exhibit C-7 from Afghan Ministry.
propositions.quote: The claimant alleged that she was a XXXX in Afghanistan. In fact, this is a significant part of her claim. To document this allegation, she presented Exhibit C-7, which purports to confirm she was a XXXX.

propositions.text: Document in English allegedly issued in Afghan language; claimant admitted substituting English without notation.
propositions.quote: She was asked why the document, allegedly issued by the Afghani Ministry XXXX XXXX XXXX, was in English. The claimant indicated that the document actually was issued in an Afghani language, but she, or her translator, substituted English for the Afghani language text. This was not noted on the document itself nor anywhere else in the file.

propositions.text: Original document not presented; claimant admitted tampering; document found not genuine.
propositions.quote: The original document was not presented. Thus, the claimant admitted that she, or those for whom she is responsible, tampered with an alleged Government document, and presented it to the Board with no explanation or notation that this had been done. The Panel thus finds this document to be not genuine, in fact this has been admitted by the claimant.

propositions.text: Submission of false document justifies negative credibility inference; document given no weight; claimant not a XXXX.
propositions.quote: From this finding flows several other findings. From the submission of a false document the panel is entitled to make a general negative inference as to credibility, and it does so. Next, this document is afforded no weight in establishing that the claimant was a XXXX. As there was no other document supplied in this regard, the Panel finds that she was not a XXXX as alleged.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant alleges being a XXXX supported by a tampered document; Panel finds document false and claimant not a XXXX.

propositions.text: Claimant alleges husband was a laborer in PIF and Exhibit R/A-2.
propositions.quote: Another key allegation of the claimant related to her husband's employment. Both in the PIF Narrative and Exhibit R/A-2 the claimant alleged that her husband was a laborer.

propositions.text: Exhibit C-11 job letter states husband was a XXXX XXXX XXXX, different from laborer.
propositions.quote: However, the job letter in Exhibit C-11 indicates that he was a XXXX XXXX XXXX which the Panel finds to be quite different from XXXX.

propositions.text: Claimant said husband was both XXXX and XXXX XXXX, adding inconsistency.
propositions.quote: When asked to explain the inconsistency, she said he was both a XXXX and XXXX XXXX, which does not explain the inconsistency, as it adds yet a third version of her alleged husband's alleged occupation.

propositions.text: Panel makes negative credibility inference; job letter given little weight; claimant's husband not employed as alleged.
propositions.quote: From this the panel makes a negative inference as to credibility, and further affords the job letter little weight, and thus finds that the claimant was not employed by the "XXXX" as alleged.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant alleges husband was laborer; job letter contradicts; claimant's inconsistent explanations reduce credibility; husband not employed as alleged.

propositions.text: Claimant alleges Taliban Commander XXXX threatened her husband; only corroboration are unsigned night letters.
propositions.quote: The claimant alleges that she was threatened by Taliban Commander XXXX, thus she had to leave Afghanistan. However, she could in no way document that this man exists, or existed, or had the alleged role in the Taliban. The only corroboration she could present were the "night letters" in Exhibit C-8.

propositions.text: Night letters not signed or mentioning commander; claimant did not report letters to police; no police report exists.
propositions.quote: However, neither of these is signed by, or mentions, this man. With respect to these letters, the claimant did not complain to the police about them, thus further corroboration that these letters were received could not be supplied by way of police report.

propositions.text: Claimant said letters omitted from Narrative because not in possession at time.
propositions.quote: The claimant was asked why she did not mention the night letters allegedly received in her Narrative, since she knew about them at the time, and she said it was because the letters were at the time not in her possession.

propositions.text: Panel finds omission of serious allegation unjustified; negative credibility inference made.
propositions.quote: However, the Panel finds, this is not sufficient reason to omit from the PIF a very serious allegation, and from this omission the panel makes a negative inference as to credibility.

propositions.text: Claimant testified husband reported night letters to police, not mentioned in Narrative; no police report exists.
propositions.quote: Further, the claimant testified that in fact her husband did report the night letters to the police, when she had not mentioned this in her Narrative, and of course there is no police report.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant alleges Taliban threats and night letters but provides no proof; omissions and contradictions reduce credibility.

propositions.text: Claimant said Taliban threatened to kill her and husband if they did not quit jobs.
propositions.quote: The claimant was asked what this man said in the three alleged threat phone calls, and she said he threatened her and her husband to quit their jobs, or they would kill the minor.

propositions.text: Claimant omitted threats to kill her and husband in testimony though in Narrative; said she might have missed it.
propositions.quote: When asked if he said anything else, she said no. However, she was asked why she failed to testify as to what she had written in her Narrative, that he had also threatened to kill the claimant and her husband. She said she might have missed that.

propositions.text: Panel rejects explanation; omission leads to negative credibility inference.
propositions.quote: However, the Panel does not accept this explanation, considering the other credibility concerns herein, and from this omission the panel makes a negative inference as to credibility.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant alleges threats to quit jobs or be killed; omitted some threats in testimony; Panel rejects explanation and doubts credibility.

propositions.text: Night letter forbade sending girls to school; claimant has no daughters; letter not addressed to her.
propositions.quote: One of the night letters referred to not sending girls to school, and the claimant was asked why she would be sent such a letter, as she had no daughters. She said the letter was not addressed to her.

propositions.text: Claimant said Taliban knows she is in touch with mothers sending children to school, explaining letter presentation.
propositions.quote: When asked, why, then, she presented the letter, she said it was because the Taliban knows that, XXXX XXXX XXXX, she is in touch with other mothers who send their children to school.

propositions.text: Panel does not accept explanation as claimant not a XXXX; finds night letters not genuine and threats did not occur.
propositions.quote: However, as the Panel has found that the claimant was not a XXXX, the Panel does not accept this explanation. As a result of all the above, and considering the other credibility concerns herein, the Panel finds that the night letters are not genuine, and that the three alleged threat calls did not actually occur.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant's explanation for night letters is rejected; Panel finds letters not genuine and threats did not occur.

propositions.text: Claimant said she quit job as XXXX in 2011 due to threats; inconsistent dates given for quitting and moving.
propositions.quote: The claimant testified that she quit her job as a XXXX as a result of the threats, and she said she did so in XXXX 2011. She was asked why she had indicated in her PIF that she left her job in XXXX 2011, and she said that she must have been confused, as she moved in XXXX 2011. Then she said she left her job in XXXX 2011.

propositions.text: Panel does not accept claimant's explanations for date inconsistencies; negative credibility inference made.
propositions.quote: It was asked of her that since she alleged that the first threat call was on XXXX XXXX, 2011, why would she have quit earlier, in XXXX or XXXX 2011? Her answer was that she was not familiar with dates. However, the claimant used only the Canadian calendar in her Narrative, and did not allege conversion problems with the Afghani calendar. Thus, the Panel does not accept the claimant's explanations for these inconsistencies, from which the panel makes negative inferences as to credibility.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant gave inconsistent dates for quitting job and moving; Panel rejects explanations and doubts credibility.

propositions.text: Claimant alleges husband was kidnapped; she reported to Kabul police who told her to report elsewhere; she did not.
propositions.quote: The Panel also does not accept that the claimant's husband was kidnapped as alleged. She says she went to the Kabul police to report it, who told her to go to the XXXX police to report it, but she did not.

propositions.text: No police or media reports exist to document alleged kidnapping.
propositions.quote: As a result, there is no police report, missing person's report, media article, etc., or anything else, to document this man's alleged kidnapping.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant alleges husband's kidnapping but no police or media reports exist; Panel does not accept allegation.

propositions.text: Due to credibility concerns, claimant's evidence is overall not credible and insufficient for refugee protection.
propositions.quote: As indicated above, from all the above credibility concerns, the Panel finds the claimant's evidence to be, overall, not credible, and thus insufficient to support her claim for refugee protection

paragraphs.summary: Panel finds claimant's evidence overall not credible and insufficient for refugee protection.

propositions.text: Minor's testimony that father was kidnapped and mother at risk rejected as these allegations were rejected above.
propositions.quote: Counsel questioned the minor, relatively briefly. The minor said his father was kidnapped, and his mother is at risk for being a XXXX, therefore he is at risk. However, as these allegations have been thoroughly rejected above, the Panel does not accept this argument of the minor.

paragraphs.summary: Minor's testimony about kidnapping and risk rejected as allegations were rejected above.

propositions.text: Minor said he feared Taliban recruitment as 16-year-old from Taliban stronghold and Pashto ethnicity.
propositions.quote: The minor said that he feared abduction and recruitment by the Taliban, as a 16 year old, especially since they are from XXXX, allegedly a Taliban stronghold, and that they are Pashtos, the same ethnicity as the Taliban.

propositions.text: Minor first said he was 17, then said it was a mistake; Panel doubts minor's credibility on age.
propositions.quote: However, the minor first said he was 17, which is a concern to the Panel in regard to identity, discussed above. The minor said this was a "mistake", however, the Panel notes, a teenager would easily be expected to know at least how old he is. For this reason alone the Panel has doubts about the minor's credibility.

paragraphs.summary: Minor fears Taliban recruitment but gave inconsistent age; Panel doubts minor's credibility.

propositions.text: Claimant added fear of forced recruitment for minor only at hearing end; no prior mention; Panel finds embellishment and negative credibility inference.
propositions.quote: The claimant was asked why there was an allegation, only at the very end of the hearing, that there is a fear on behalf of the minor of forced recruitment by the Taliban, when this alleged head of fear was never mentioned before in any previous submission of either claimant? She could provide no explanation, thus the Panel finds even the addition of this alleged head of fear to be an embellishment at the hearing, from which the panel makes a negative inference as to credibility.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant added minor's forced recruitment fear late without explanation; Panel finds embellishment and doubts credibility.

propositions.text: Claimant is female; some risk exists for females in Afghanistan without male protection.
propositions.quote: However, it is evident the claimant is female, and the Panel notes from the documentation before it that there may be some risk or vulnerability for females living in Afghanistan without the protection of male family members.

propositions.text: Panel cannot accept claimant would be without husband if returned; no persecution for this reason.
propositions.quote: As indicated above, for credibility concerns, the Panel cannot even accept that the claimant would be without a husband if she hypothetically returned to Afghanistan, thus the Panel finds that the claimant would not be subject to persecution for this reason.

paragraphs.summary: Panel notes some risk for females without male protection but does not accept claimant would be without husband; no persecution found.

propositions.text: The Taliban could hypothetically target any females in Afghanistan for kidnapping or dress code violations.
propositions.quote: It is hypothetically possible that the Taliban could target any females in Afghanistan, for kidnapping or even for not dressing in a fully Islamic fashion.

propositions.text: No allegation or convincing evidence shows such targeting has happened or worsened since 2011 when claimants left Afghanistan.
propositions.quote: There was no allegation that this has happened in the past, nor any convincing evidence that the situation has deteriorated significantly since 2011 when the claimants left Afghanistan.

propositions.text: No evidence or argument shows the female claimant is more likely a Taliban target than other Afghan females.
propositions.quote: no persuasive evidence or argument has been adduced, nor is the Panel aware of any, that would make the female claimant more of a hypothetical target of the Taliban or other such potential agents of persecution than any other female Afghans.

propositions.text: No allegation that the family is high profile or politically opposed to Taliban; prior claims about claimant's and husband's roles were rejected.
propositions.quote: There was not any allegation that the family is of particularly high profile that would attract the attention of the Taliban or others, and, it is recalled, the allegations that the claimant was a XXXX and her husband worked for "XXXX" were rejected.

propositions.text: No evidence family publicly opposed Taliban or supported West or government.
propositions.quote: No evidence was submitted that the family publicly expressed any political opinion opposed to the Taliban, or for the West of the Government.

propositions.text: Taliban could hypothetically target anyone in Afghanistan, but no evidence shows claimants are more likely targets than others.
propositions.quote: it is conceivably possible that the minor could be kidnapped by the Taliban for the purpose of forced recruitment, but there is insufficient evidence to suggest that this is anything more that a mere possibility, and the Panel finds that there is not even a serious possibility that the minor would be persecuted for this or any other reason upon a hypothetical return to Afghanistan.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Taliban could hypothetically target females, but no evidence shows claimants are more likely targets or persecuted than others since 2011.

propositions.text: The Panel finds claimants are not Convention refugees under s. 96 nor persons in need of protection under s. 97 of IRPA.
propositions.quote: the Panel finds the claimants to not be Convention refugees under s. 96 nor persons in need of protection under s. 97 of the IRPA.

propositions.text: The claims are rejected with respect to all claimants for the reasons noted above.
propositions.quote: the claims are rejected with respect to all claimants.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes claimants are not refugees or in need of protection and rejects all claims accordingly.
